sentences.text: This predator possessed very short but functional forelimbs ending in four fingers, the first three of which bore sharp claws.

The Cleveland-Lloyd specimen is one of the largest known individuals, yet the Colorado skull was found disarticulated, strongly flattened sideways, and showed unfused sutures indicating it had not reached full adult size.
One species name, C. magnicornis, specifically refers to a larger nasal horn.

The genus was first described by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1884 based on a nearly complete skeleton found in Garden Park, Colorado, within the Morrison Formation. The holotype specimen USNM 4735 was excavated by farmer Marshall Parker Felch in 1883 and 1884, though it was encased in hard sandstone that caused significant distortion of the skull and spine during fossilization.

While some researchers once suggested it hunted aquatic prey like fish, recent studies reject this in favor of it preying on plant-eating dinosaurs. Oswald and Curtice (2026) argue that the dentition of Ceratosaurus might have been an adaptation for quickly killing medium-sized prey.

Ceratosaurus belongs to the parent group Ceratosauria. In 2000, Madsen and Welles described two new species, C. dentisulcatus and C. magnicornis, but as of 2025, these are generally considered synonyms of C. nasicornis. Brooks Britt and colleagues suggested in 2000 that C. nasicornis is a juvenile and that the others represent the adult form of a single species. In 2015, Elisabete Malafaia and colleagues assigned a Portuguese specimen to Ceratosaurus aff. C. nasicornis after questioning the validity of C. dentisulcatus.

Ceratosaurus lived during the Late Jurassic period, approximately 155 million years ago, in North America and Europe. More precise dating places it in the late Jurassic Period, approximately 153 to 148 million years ago, in the Kimmeridgian and Tithonian stages. Fossils have been found in what is now North America, Africa, Uruguay, and Europe.

Most paleontologists no longer accept C. dentisulcatus and C. magnicornis as valid species, suggesting the skeletons may represent different growth stages of C. nasicornis. It is debated whether fragmentary remains from Tanzania, Uruguay, and Switzerland belong to Ceratosaurus, as most paleontologists do not currently accept this assignment. It is also debated whether the nasal horn was a weapon as Marsh originally suggested, with modern views favoring its use for display only. Brooks Britt and colleagues suggested in 2000 that C. nasicornis is a juvenile and that C. dentisulcatus and C. magnicornis represent the adult form of a single species.
